To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the principles of classification provide necessary conditions for a good class structure, and that multiple class structures are possible.

the quality of a set of classes is evaluated by considering the extent to which they satisfy four principles of classification: (i) they are based on a set of properties, which are relevant and sufficient for the purpose at hand; (ii) the properties are grouped into classes that are mutually exclusive, and the classes are collectively exhaustive; (iii) the class structure is consistent with the way the domain is perceived by the user; and (iv) there are no superfluous classes.

(1) classes are a means to classify instances in order to provide a cognitive economy and to make inferences about classified items in the absence of full information; (2) classes are defined over sets of instances, which can be represented by a set of attributes; (3) classes have an associated set of attributes, and (4) the set of classes can be represented as a set of classes and a class structure.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how to decide which classes to use in a data model, and how to decide when to stop adding more classes.
providing guidelines that will assist in the design of classes for data models and, in particular, object-oriented models.
the evaluation of class structures, not individual classes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a class is a set of instances with a structure that satisfies the principles of classification.
the classes in a model are a good representation of the domain of interest if they are a potential class and are structured in accordance with the principles of classification.
the principles of classification provide a set of necessary conditions for a class structure to be considered good.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the notion of class is not well defined in the current literature.
classes should be chosen so as to support human cognition.
the notion of class should be used to model an application only when it is possible to identify a class structure over the domain.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the principles of classification provide a theoretical basis for the selection and evaluation of classes.
the quality of classes is a critical aspect of data modeling that has not been sufficiently addressed.
the notion of a good set of classes is not arbitrary and can be defined based on cognitive principles.
